title: Brioche cowl
subtitle: A plush single-colour brioche rib worked in the round.
excerpt: A cowl knitted in the round in single-colour brioche stitch on 5.5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 60 cm circumference and 26 cm tall. The brioche rib is approximately twice as thick as a standard 1x1 rib in the same yarn and gives a soft, pillowy cowl that compresses into a small pack when not worn.
sourceNotes: Single-colour brioche in the round draws on Victorian brioche-stitch techniques documented in Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive, under the names brioche rib and sailor stitch. Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) documents the slip-stitch-with-yarn-over technique, citations only.
heroPrompt: A finished brioche cowl in heathered grey aran-weight yarn, photographed lying flat on a pale surface showing the lofty puffed rib texture, with the round tube shape visible.

glossaryTerms.definition: A stitch pattern in which every alternate stitch is slipped with a yarn-over on one pass, then the slipped stitch and its yarn-over are worked together as one on the return pass, creating a tall, pillowy rib.
Knit the slipped stitch together with its paired yarn-over from the previous round as a single stitch.
Bring yarn to the front, slip next stitch purlwise to right needle, carry yarn over right needle tip to back. The slip and yarn-over sit together as a paired unit.
Knitting a small circumference in the round on one long circular needle by pulling a loop of cable through the stitches at the halfway point.
A cast-on forming a neat elastic edge by using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a cowl knitted in the round in single-colour
brioche stitch
on 5.5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 60 cm circumference and 26 cm tall. In the round, brioche uses a two-round repeat: round 1 works
BrK
and
sl1yo
alternating, and round 2 swaps their positions. The yarn-over accumulated in round 1 is consumed in round 2, and the rib never needs purling.

In-the-round construction was chosen because brioche in the round eliminates the BrP (brioche purl) entirely: both rounds use knit-based operations, which makes the in-the-round version easier to work than the flat version. The
magic loop
on an 80 cm circular needle handles 90 stitches well. The finished cowl needs about 350 m (approximately 220 g) of aran-weight yarn.
What you need

items.name: Aran-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Any aran-weight yarn. Wool gives the most loft for brioche.

content.text: Gauge

15 sts x 20 rounds = 10 x 10 cm in single-colour brioche in the round on 5.5 mm needles, unblocked. The brioche gauge counts working stitches only, not the yarn-overs. Swatch the two-round brioche repeat in the round, measure working stitch columns across the relaxed centre. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished circumference by approximately 4 cm at this stitch count.
Stitches used
Sl1yo: bring yarn to front, slip next stitch purlwise, carry yarn over right needle tip to back.
BrK: insert right needle knitwise through slipped stitch and its yarn-over together, wrap yarn, draw through as one stitch.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 90 stitches on the needle. The stitch count must be even for 1x1 brioche in the round: 90 = 45 pairs. Before beginning, calculate the tail: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5.5 mm needles (circumference approximately 17.3 mm) and 90 stitches: (17.3 x 90) / 10 + 15 = 155.7 + 15 = about 171 cm. Leave at least 171 cm of tail.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 90 stitches. Join to work in the round. Place a stitch marker.
Body
Set-up round: *Sl1yo, K1; repeat from * to end. (90 sts)
Round 1: *BrK, Sl1yo; repeat from * to end. (90 sts)
Round 2: *Sl1yo, BrK; repeat from * to end. (90 sts)

Repeat rounds 1 and 2 until the cowl measures 26 cm from the cast-on. Note that brioche in the round can lengthen by 10 to 15 percent when relaxed; measure with the cowl lying flat on a table rather than hanging. At the halfway mark (approximately round 26 of the 52 body rounds), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at round 26 you should have 90 working stitches on the needle.
Bind off
Work a stretchy bind-off: BrK the first brioche stitch, *slip result back to left needle, K2tog tbl; repeat from * to end. Cut yarn and draw through the last loop.
Common faults

Stitch count rising. The sl1yo and BrK must alternate exactly: each sl1yo from the previous round must be consumed as a BrK on the next, and each K from the previous round must become a sl1yo. If you BrK a stitch that was already a plain K, you consume no extra stitch but work an extra loop, raising the count.

Rounds 1 and 2 swapping by accident. The two rounds differ only in which stitches begin with BrK versus sl1yo. If the rounds swap, the brioche columns suddenly sit between the rib valleys rather than on top of them. Use a stitch marker of different colours for rounds 1 and 2 if needed.
Brioche appears flat and thin. Usually a needle size problem. The aran-weight yarn on 5.5 mm needles should produce an airy brioche. If the fabric looks compressed, try 6 mm needles for the swatch.
Finishing
Weave in both tails at the cast-on join and bind-off edge. Do not block. The loft of brioche is irreversibly lost if wet blocked.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Press out water gently. Lay flat over a round form to dry. Do not tumble dry or stretch while damp.
What to try next

The brioche scarf applies the same stitch in flat construction, using the BrP on wrong-side rows. The two-colour brioche scarf introduces a second yarn colour worked on alternating rows for a reversible two-faced piece.
